newsitem.title: USA: States gear up for possible tobacco accord.
newsitem.headline: States gear up for possible tobacco accord.

text.p: The nation's state attorneys general have escalated talks about what should be included in any settlement of massive litigation against the tobacco industry amid speculation such a deal could come before a key trial set for June.

Former Maine Attorney General James Tierney, who is coordinating state litigation efforts, told Reuters that while the lead states are preparing for trial, they also think the industry is seriously weighing the risks of a courtroom battle.

He said that while talks among some attorneys general, the health community and some Congress members have been increasing, they have held no direct talks with tobacco industry officials. Tierney denied published reports that the attorneys general have held meetings in the last few months with tobacco representatives in Washington and Memphis, Tenn.
He also cautioned that the possibility of a settlement proposal is strictly speculation at this point and that it could be a long time before any such agreement is reached.

More than 20 lawsuits have been filed by states, cities and counties against the tobacco industry aimed at recouping the Medicare costs of smokers. The first of those trials, brought by Mississippi's attorney general, is set to begin in June in Pascagoula.

"We (attorneys general) know we are going to trial in the next six months. ... We also know the tobacco industry is not stupid, so it would be wrong for the a.g.'s not to prepare themselves in some way for what might be coming along from the tobacco industry in the next three or four months."
"You have to ask yourself, 'Does the whole tobacco industry want to roll the dice on the decision of a single chancery judge in a small town in Mississippi?'"
Speculation has been steadily rising that the industry is taking an active look at a possible settlement, causing some attorneys general, who have opposed a settlement, to take defensive actions.

One of the most visible, Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey III, sent a letter earlier this month to tobacco litigants and health officials saying he met with key members of Congress to discuss standards he would want if a settlement should be offered.
"We wanted to draw a line in the sand," said Joe Loveland, a Humphrey spokesman.

Rumours over a possible industry proposal swirled last week when Wall Street brokerage Sanford C. Bernstein issued a research report saying the industry was likely to agree to be regulated by the government and to pay into a settlement fund in exchange for a settlement protecting companies from any future claims for illnesses caused by smoking.

Such speculation was also fuelled by the fact that cigarette companies recently hired two politically well-connected Washington law firms and Bozell, Sawyer, Miller Group, a powerful public relations firm, to handle tobacco litigation matters.

The National Journal, a well-respected Washington publication, reported last week the firms had been hired specifically to develop plans for a comprehenisve settlement of the industry's legal and regulatory problems.
Philip Morris Cos Inc. and R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. referred all questions about the story to Bozell, Sawyer.
Lance Morgan, a spokesman at Bozell, confirmed the firms had been hired to help with litigation, regulatory and possibly legislative issues.
However, he added, "Neither the attorneys general nor the plaintiffs' lawyers have proposed a comprehensive settlement to the industry nor has the industry proposed one."
